label: t1
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{t1}
    A full order in a quaternion division algebra over a local field $K$ is a ghost 
    intersection of maximal orders if and only if its Gorenstein closure is a Bass 
    order.
head: environment

title: Corollary
body_md:
If $\{\mathbf R_i\}_{i\in I}$ is a finite family of orders having a Bass 
    Gorenstein closure, then the intersection $\bigcup_{i\in I}\mathbf R_i$ has the
    same property.\qed
head: environment

label: d1
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{d1}
    Let $\mathfrak{Q}$ be either $\mathfrak{A}_0$ or $\mathfrak{A}$, let 
    $\mathfrak{L}\subset\mathfrak{Q}$ be a two-dimensional semisimple commutative 
    algebra whose unique maximal order is $\mathcal{O}_{\mathfrak{L}}$, let 
    $\mathbf{H}\subset\mathfrak{Q}$ be a full order,
    and let $\mathfrak{Q}_*=\mathfrak{Q}\smallsetminus K$, as before. 
    Let $n=n(\mathfrak{L},\mathbf{H})$ be the 
    non-negative integer satisfying 
    $\mathfrak{L}\cap\mathbf{H}=\mathcal{O}_{\mathfrak{L}}^{[n]}$. For any semisimple 
    element $a\in\mathfrak{Q}_*$ and for any full 
    order $\mathbf{H}$,
    we write $n(a,\mathbf{H})$ for $n(K[a],\mathbf{H})$. We also set $m(a)=m$ for 
    the integer satisfying $\mathcal{O}_K[a]=\mathcal{O}_{K[a]}^{[m]}$. Note that
    $a\in\mathbf{H}$ is equivalent to $m(a)\geq n(a,\mathbf{H})$.
head: environment

title: Proposition
body_md:
Every element $a\in\mathfrak{A}_*$ is semisimple.
    Two full orders $\mathbf{H}$ and $\mathbf{H}'$ in $\mathfrak{Q}=\mathfrak{A}$ are equal if and only if
    $n(a,\mathbf{H})=n(a,\mathbf{H}')$ for any element $a\in\mathfrak{Q}_*$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The first statement is well known, since every element
    $a\in\mathfrak{A}_*$ generates a field. 
    By the last statement in Def. \ref{d1}, the condition $n(a,\mathbf{H})=n(a,\mathbf{H}')$
    implies that $a\in\mathbf{H}$ if and only if $a\in\mathbf{H}'$. The result
    follows since $K\cap\mathbf{H}=\mathcal{O}_K$ for every order $\mathbf{H}$.
head: environment

title: Proposition
body_md:
Let $\mathfrak{L}\subset\mathfrak{A}_0$ be a two dimensional semisimple 
    commutative algebra and let $m\geq0$ be arbitrary. 
    Then $n(\mathfrak{L},\mathbf{D})=0$, for a maximal order $\mathbf{D}$, if and only
    if $\mathbf{D}$ is a stem order of $\mathcal{O}_{\mathfrak{L}}^{[m]}$.
    Furthermore, if two neighboring maximal orders, $\mathbf{D}$ and $\mathbf{D}'$
    satisfy $n(\mathfrak{L},\mathbf{D})=n(\mathfrak{L},\mathbf{D}')$ then 
    $n(\mathfrak{L},\mathbf{D})=0$. If $n(\mathfrak{L},\mathbf{D})=n>0$, then
    $\mathbf{D}$ has a unique neighbor $\mathbf{D}'$ such that 
    $n(\mathfrak{L},\mathbf{D}')=n-1$. Any other neighbor $\mathbf{D}''$ satisfies 
    $n(\mathfrak{L},\mathbf{D}'')=n+1$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The first statement is immediate from the definition of stem order. 
    Note that the stem vertices are independent of $m$, and are the vertices
    of a path, which is a subtree. For any maximal order that is not a stem order
    of $\mathcal{O}_{\mathfrak{L}}^{[m]}$, there is a unique path connecting it
    to the closest stem vertex. This path goes through a unique neighbor,
    which might be a stem vertex itself. This neighbor is one unit closer to the
    set of stem vertices, while all the others are farther away. In particular,
    no neighbor is at the same distance.
head: environment

title: Corollary
body_md:
Let $\mathfrak{L}\subset\mathfrak{A}_0$ be a two dimensional semisimple 
    commutative algebra. Consider a sequence $\mathbf{D}_0,\mathbf{D}_1,\dots,\mathbf{D}_n$ of maximal orders
    satisfying the following conditions:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $n(\mathfrak{L},\mathbf{D}_0)=0$,
        \item $\mathbf{D}_i$ and $\mathbf{D}_{i+1}$ are neighbors for $0\leq i\leq n-1$,
        and 
        \item $\mathbf{D}_i\neq\mathbf{D}_{i+2}$ for $0\leq i\leq n-2$.
    \end{itemize}
    Then, there is an integer $r$ with $0\leq r\leq n$ such that $n(\mathfrak{L},\mathbf{D}_i)=0$, 
    for $0\leq i\leq r$, and 
    $n(\mathfrak{L},\mathbf{D}_i)=i-r$, for $r\leq i\leq n$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $\mathbf{D}_i$ and $\mathbf{D}_{i+1}$ are neighbors, it is clear that
    $n(\mathfrak{L},\mathbf{D}_i)$ and $n(\mathfrak{L},\mathbf{D}_{i+1})$ differ
    by $1$ at most, and they are equal if and only if they are both $0$. Let $r$
    be the largest integer such that $n(\mathfrak{L},\mathbf{D}_i)=0$ for
    $0\leq i\leq r$. If $r=n$, there is nothing to prove. If $r<n$, then
    $n(\mathfrak{L},\mathbf{D}_{r+1})=1$. If $r<n-1$, we must have
    $n(\mathfrak{L},\mathbf{D}_{r+2})=2$ since there is exactly one neighbor $\mathbf{D}$
    of $\mathbf{D}_{r+1}$ satisfying $n(\mathfrak{L},\mathbf{D})=0$, and it is 
    $\mathbf{D}=\mathbf{D}_r$. Iterations are analogous.
head: environment

label: p25
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{p25}
    Let $E/K$ be a finite extension and let $e=e(E/K)$ be its ramification degree.
    Let $a\in\mathfrak{Q}_*$ be a semisimple element whose image 
    $a_E\in \mathfrak{Q}_E$ is also semisimple. 
    Then, we have $m(a_E)=em(a)+b$
    for some constant $b=b(\mathfrak{L})$ depending 
    only on the isomorphism class of $\mathfrak{L}=K[a]$. Furthermore, if 
    $n=n(a_E,\mathbf{S})$ and $n_1=n(a,\mathfrak{Q}\cap\mathbf{S})$,
    for a full order $\mathbf{S}\subset\mathfrak{Q}_E$, then $e(n_1-1)+b<n\leq en_1+b$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since every order in $\mathfrak{L}_E$ has the form 
    $\mathcal{O}_{\mathfrak{L}_E}^{[s]}$, for some $s\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq0}$, we can 
    define $b$ by the relation $(\mathcal{O}_{\mathfrak{L}})_E=
    \mathcal{O}_{\mathfrak{L}_E}^{[b]}$. The first statement follows since 
    $\pi_K=u\pi_E^e$ for some unit $u\in\mathcal{O}_E^*$. For the second statement,
    note that $K[a]$ has integral generators $a'$ and $a''$ satisfying $m(a')=n-1$
    and $m(a')=n$. This means that $a'\in\mathfrak{Q}\cap\mathbf{S}$, while $a''\notin\mathfrak{Q}\cap\mathbf{S}$. This implies $a_E'\in\mathbf{S}$ and
    $a_E''\notin\mathbf{S}$. The result follows.
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md:
A full order $\mathbf B\subseteq\mathfrak{A}$ is Bass if and only if $\mathbf B\not\subset
    \mathcal{O}_{\mathfrak{A}}^{[1]}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If $\mathbf B\subseteq\mathcal{O}_{\mathfrak{A}}^{[1]}$, then $\mathbf B$ is not Bass by
    definition, since $\mathcal{O}_{\mathfrak{A}}^{[1]}$ is not Gorenstein. On the
    other hand, if $\mathbf B$ is not Bass, then $\mathbf B\subset\mathbf R^{[1]}$ for
    some order $\mathbf R$, but $\mathbf R^{[1]}\subseteq\mathcal{O}_{\mathfrak{A}}^{[1]}$,
    since $\mathbf R\subseteq\mathcal{O}_{\mathfrak{A}}$.
head: environment

label: l32
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{l32}
    Let $L/K$ be the unique unramified quadratic extension.
    If $\mathbf B\subseteq\mathfrak{A}$ is a Bass order, the $\mathcal{O}_L$-order $\mathbf B_L\subset
    \mathfrak{A}_L$ generated by $\mathbf B$ is a Bass order.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $\mathbf B$ is Bass, it follows from the preceding lemma that there is an element
    $b\in\mathbf B$ that does not belong to $\mathcal{O}_{\mathfrak{A}}^{[1]}$. In particular, the
    order $\mathbf{H}=\mathcal{O}_K[b]\subset K[b]$ is maximal in the latter subfield. Choosing
    a different generator of the commutative order if needed, we can assume that $b$
    is either a uniformizing parameter in a ramified quadratic extension, or a unit
    generating an unramified quadratic extension whose image on the residue field satisfies $\mathbb{K}[\bar{b}]\neq\mathbb{K}$.

    In the first case, $b_L$ is still a uniformizing parameter in a ramified quadratic
    extension $L[b_L]$ of $L$. It follows from  \cite[Prop. 4.2]{Eichler2} that
    its branch $\mathfrak{s}_L(b_L)$ is an edge. In particular, the branch $\mathfrak{s}_L(\mathbf B_L)$
    is contained in an edge. It follows from \cite[Th. 1.2]{A26}
    that $\mathfrak{s}_L(\mathbf B_L)$ is Bass.

    In the second case we have $L[b_L]\cong L\times L$, since the eigenvalues of $b$ are
    in $L$. Under this isomorphism $b_L$ corresponds to a pair of the form 
    $(\lambda,\bar{\lambda})$, where $\bar{\lambda}$ is the image of $\lambda$
    under the non-trivial $K$-automorphism of $L$. Since $\mathbb{K}[\bar{b}]\neq
    \mathbb{K}$, $\nu_L(\lambda-\bar{\lambda})=0$, which implies by 
    \cite[Prop. 4.2]{Eichler2} that $\mathfrak{s}_L(b)$ is a maximal path. Now the
    result follows as before.
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md:
Let $L/K$ be the unique unramified quadratic extension. Then for any full order
    $\mathbf R\subset\mathfrak{A}$ we have $(\mathbf R^{[r]})_L=(\mathbf R_L)^{[r]}$. In particular, if the
    Gorenstein closure of $\mathbf R$ is a Bass order, the same holds for $\mathbf R_L$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $L/K$ is unramified, $\pi_K$ is also a uniformizing parameter
    for $L$. It follows that 
    $$(\mathbf R^{[r]})_L=(\mathcal{O}_K+\pi_K^r\mathbf R)_L=
    \mathcal{O}_L(\mathcal{O}_K+\pi_K^r\mathbf R)=
    \mathcal{O}_L+\pi_K^r(\mathcal{O}_L\mathbf R)=(\mathbf R_L)^{[r]}.$$
    For the last statement, if the Gorenstein closure $\mathbf R_0$
    of $\mathbf R$ is Bass, then $\mathbf R=\mathbf R_0^{[m]}$ for some integer
    $m\geq0$. Furthermore, $(\mathbf R_0)_L$ is Bass by the preceding result, and we have $\mathbf R_L=(\mathbf R_0^{[m]})_L=
    (\mathbf R_0)^{[m]}_L$, whence the result follows.
head: environment

label: p34
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since the Gorenstein closure of $\mathbf R$ is a Bass order, the same holds for $\mathbf R_L$
    by the preceding lemma. Since $\mathfrak{A}_L$ is a matrix algebra, then $\mathbf R_L$
    is a ghost intersection of maximal orders by \cite[Th. 1.1]{A26}. 
    This means that $\mathbf R_L=\mathfrak{A}_L\cap\bigcap_{j\in J}\mathbf{D}_j$ for some collection
    $\{\mathbf{D}_j|j\in J\}$ of maximal orders in $\mathfrak{A}_E$, for some extension $E/L$.
    Then $$\mathbf R=\mathfrak{A}\cap\mathbf R_L=\mathfrak{A}\cap\bigcap_{j\in J}\mathbf{D}_j,$$
    as claimed.
head: environment

label: p35
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{p35}
    Write $\mathbf R=\mathbf R_1^{[r]}$, with $r>0$, for a non-Gorenstein order $\mathbf R$. With this notation, if $\mathbf R$
    is a ghost intersection of maximal orders, then
    so is $\mathbf R_1$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By induction, it suffices to assume $r=1$.  Note that 
    $\mathbf R\subseteq\mathcal{O}_{\mathfrak{A}}^{[1]}$, whence,
    $n(a,\mathbf R)\geq 1$ for any $a\in\mathfrak{A}_*=
    \mathfrak{A}\smallsetminus K$. Write 
    $\mathbf R=\mathfrak{A}\cap\mathbf{S}$, where $\mathbf{S}=\bigcap_{j\in J}\mathbf{D}_j$
    is a full order in $\mathfrak{A}_E$ that can be written as the intersection of some
    collection $\{\mathbf{D}_j\}_{j\in J}$ of maximal orders in $\mathfrak{A}_E$ 
    for some finite 
    extension $E/K$.  Fix a maximal order $\mathbf{D}$ in $\mathfrak{A}_E$ containing 
    $\mathcal{O}_{\mathfrak{A}}$. Then $n(a_E,\mathbf{D})\leq b(a)$,
    if $b(a)=b(K\big(a)\big)$ as in Prop. \ref{p25}, for any 
    $a\in\mathfrak{A}_*$. Let $e=e(E/K)$. For every order $\mathbf{D}_j$ 
    in the collection we choose a maximal order $\mathbf{D}'_j$ as follows: 
    \begin{itemize} \item If the distance
    in the Bruhat-Tits tree of $\mathfrak{A}_E$ between the vertices corresponding to
    $\mathbf{D}_j$ and $\mathbf{D}$ is $e$ or less, we set $\mathbf{D}'_j=\mathbf{D}$,
    \item otherwise we choose $\mathbf{D}'_j$ as the maximal order corresponding to a vertex
    in the path between $v_{\mathbf{D}}$ and $v_{\mathbf{D}_j}$ at distance $e$ from
    $v_{\mathbf{D}_j}$. \end{itemize}
    Let $\mathbf{S}'=\bigcap_{j\in J}\mathbf{D}'_j$.
    It suffices to show that $n(a,\mathfrak{A}\cap\mathbf{S})=n(a,\mathfrak{A}\cap\mathbf{S}')+1$
    for every $a\in\mathfrak{A}_*$. To prove this we note that 
    $n(a_E,\mathbf{D})\leq b(a)$. For any $j\in J$, we have two cases:
    \begin{itemize} \item If $n(a_E,\mathbf{D}'_j)\leq b(a)$, then
    $n(a_E,\mathbf{D}_j)\leq b(a)+e$ since $d(v_{\mathbf{D}},v_{\mathbf{D}_j})\leq e$.
    In this case $n(a,\mathfrak{A}\cap\mathbf{D}_j)\leq 1$ and $n(a,\mathfrak{A}\cap\mathbf{D}'_j)=0$.
    \item If $n(a_E,\mathbf{D}'_j)> b(a)\geq0$, then $\mathbf{D}'_j\neq
    \mathbf{D}$, whence $d(v_{\mathbf{D}'_j},v_{\mathbf{D}_j})=e$. Then $n(a_E,\mathbf{D}_j)=
    n(a_E,\mathbf{D}'_j)+e$. This implies $n(a,\mathfrak{A}\cap\mathbf{D}_j)=
    n(a,\mathfrak{A}\cap\mathbf{D}'_j)+1$.
    \end{itemize}
    We conclude that $n(a,\mathfrak{A}\cap\mathbf{D}_j)=n(a,\mathfrak{A}\cap\mathbf{D}'_j)+1$ unless
    $n(a,\mathfrak{A}\cap\mathbf{D}_j)=n(a,\mathfrak{A}\cap\mathbf{D}'_j)=0$. The condition $n(a,\mathbf R)\geq 1$
    show that these values of $j$ are not relevant to compute $n(a,\mathbf R)=
    \max_{j\in J}n(a,\mathfrak{A}\cap\mathbf{D}_j)$, and they can be ignored. The result follows.
head: environment

label: p36
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If $\mathbf R$ is not a Bass order, then $\mathbf R\subseteq\mathcal{O}_{\mathfrak{A}}^{[1]}$. 
    Write $\mathbf R=\mathfrak{A}\cap\mathbf{S}$, where $\mathbf{S}=\bigcap_{j\in J}\mathbf{D}_j$, 
    and define $\mathbf{S}'$ as in the preceding proof. Then the same 
    computation as before shows $n(a,\mathbf R)=n(a,\mathfrak{A}\cap\mathbf{S}')+1$ for 
    all $a\in\mathfrak{A}_*$. It follows that 
    $\mathbf R_1=\mathfrak{A}\cap\mathbf{S}'$ satisfies $\mathbf R=\mathbf R_1^{[1]}$. This 
    contradicts the fact that $\mathbf R$ is Gorenstein, concluding the proof.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If the Gorenstein closure of $\mathbf R$ is Bass, it follows from Prop.
    \ref{p34} that $\mathbf R$ is a ghost intersection of maximal orders. 
    On the other hand, if $\mathbf R$ is a ghost intersection
    of maximal orders, so is its Gorenstein closure
    $\mathbf R'$ by Prop. \ref{p35}. Now Prop. \ref{p36} shows that $\mathbf R'$
    is Bass.
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md:
Let R be a ring, and let $\Lambda_0 \subset \Lambda_1$ be two R-modules 
 satisfying $\Lambda_1/\Lambda_0\cong R$ as $R$-modules. Then every 
 $R$-submodule of $\Lambda_1$ containing $\Lambda_0$ equals $I\Lambda_1 
 + \Lambda_0$ for some ideal $I$ of $R$. In particular, if
$R$ is a principal ideal domain, then every $R$-submodule of $\Lambda_1$ 
containing $\Lambda_0$ equals $a\Lambda_1 + \Lambda_0$, for some
element $a\in R$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
It is immediate from the correspondence theorem that all the considered  
    submodules have the form $\Lambda_2/\Lambda_0$, where 
    $\Lambda_0\subseteq\Lambda_2\subseteq\Lambda_1$. Since the 
    $R$-submodules of $R$ are precisely the ideals, the result follows from 
    the identity $I(\Lambda_1/\Lambda_0)=I\Lambda_1+\Lambda_0$.
head: environment
